summary: For ages 9-10: pupils recognise that in a multi-digit whole number a digit in one place is worth ten times what the same digit is worth in the place to its right (and one-tenth of the same digit in the place to its left). The 3 in 3,000 is ten times the 3 in 300; 700 ÷ 70 = 10. The aim is to name the multiplicative ×10 structure between adjacent places that has been implicit since 'ten ones make a ten', and to hold it alongside the additive (partition) view. A central scaffold is a place-value / Gattegno chart where moving a digit one column left multiplies its value by 10 and one column right divides it by 10; a static or paper chart with counters can serve the same purpose.
misconceptions: Seeing place value only additively and missing the ×10 relationship between places.
Thinking the 3 in 3,000 is '10 more' than in 300 rather than 10 times.
Confusing 'ten times' with 'add a zero' as a meaningless trick (fails for decimals later).
Miscounting the factor across non-adjacent places (×10 vs ×100).
Not connecting 700÷70=10 to the adjacent-place relationship.

activities.title: Slide a digit across the place-value chart
steps: Set up a place-value chart with columns for ones, tens, hundreds, thousands (and more).
Place a single digit — say a 3 — in the hundreds column so it is worth 300.

Move that same 3 one column to the LEFT and state its new value (3,000). Say what happened to the value and by how much: it became ten TIMES as much, not 'ten more'. (For whole numbers the written numeral also gains a zero, but that is a by-product — the reason is the ×10 in value.)
Move the 3 back to the RIGHT (÷10): from 3,000, one column right returns it to 300, and a further column right makes it 30.
Write the matching sentence each time, e.g. 300 × 10 = 3,000 and 3,000 ÷ 10 = 300.
activities.insight: Shifting a digit one place left multiplies its value by 10 and one place right divides it by 10; place value is multiplicative between adjacent columns, not merely 'adding a zero'.

activities.title: How many times greater? Counting the place-shifts
steps: Compare the same digit in two different places, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 and the 5 in 5,000.
Slide one placement of the 5 towards the other, counting the number of column hops.
State the factor: one hop = ×10, so the 5 in 50,000 is ten times the 5 in 5,000.
Repeat for a non-adjacent pair, e.g. the 5 in 50,000 compared with the 5 in 500: count the hops (two), so the factor is ×10×10 = ×100.
Say in words how many times greater, and justify by the number of place-shifts.
activities.insight: The factor between two placements of a digit equals ten raised to the number of column shifts: one shift is ×10, two shifts is ×100. Non-adjacent places are not automatically 'ten times'.

activities.title: Division and multiplication sentences as the place-value step
steps: Complete 700 ÷ 70 = ___ and explain the answer using place names, not just the computed digits.
Explain how 700 ÷ 70 = 10 connects to 70 and 700 sitting in adjacent place-value columns (the 7 in 700 is one place to the left of the 7 in 70, so 700 is ten times as much as 70).
Write a few matched pairs showing both directions, e.g. 30 = 3 × 10 and 3 = 30 ÷ 10.
Point to or highlight the two adjacent columns involved for each sentence so the quotient of 10 is seen as a single left/right place step.
activities.insight: Division and multiplication sentences such as 700 ÷ 70 = 10 express the adjacent-place relationship itself: moving one place is ×10 or ÷10.

activities.title: Ten times or ten more? Correcting the claim
steps: Consider a claim that 'the 3 in 3,000 is ten MORE than the 3 in 300' and decide whether it is right.
Explain why it is wrong and restate it correctly as 'ten TIMES'.
Support the correction with evidence: 300 × 10 = 3,000, or ten stacks of 300 reaching 3,000, or the single left-shift on the chart.
Preview the right-hand direction: a dimmed column to the right of the ones is where tenths will later live (the ÷10 direction continues past the ones).
activities.insight: 'Ten times' (multiplicative) and 'ten more' (additive) are different; place value is multiplicative, which is why the pattern extends consistently into decimals.

checkQuestion: Write 300 and 3,000 side by side. Point to the 3 in each. Ask: 'The value of this 3 compared with that 3 — how many times bigger is one than the other? How do you know?'
checkAnswer: Ten times bigger. Each place to the left is worth ten times the place to its right, and 3,000 is one place to the left of 300, so its 3 is worth ten times as much.
